name: Mechanical traction table

card.summary: A motorised table that gently stretches the spine, used in looksmaxxing circles in the hope of decompressing discs and recovering a little standing height or posture.
card.aka: Traction table, DRX9000, spinal decompression table
card.note: Clinical traction is studied for back pain, not for adult height gain; surgical traction tables carry documented nerve and soft-tissue risks.

quick.overview:
A mechanical traction table is a motorised table that applies a controlled pulling force to the spine, often marketed as non-surgical spinal decompression (the DRX9000 is a well-known brand). In height-focused communities it is discussed as a way to decompress the discs and make the most of the spine's full length.

Clinical studies of such devices look at back pain and disc height rather than adult stature. One retrospective cohort reported that restored disc height after a course of motorised decompression went along with less discogenic low back pain [1]. Measured height also naturally varies by roughly a centimetre or more across a day [3].
quick.how: Sessions are typically delivered in a physiotherapy or chiropractic clinic over a series of weeks, with the person lying on the table in a harness while the device cycles pulling force. Some people in height communities pair traction or inversion with posture and core work.
quick.risks: Clinic traction is generally used for back and neck conditions. In surgical settings, traction tables have been linked to perineal skin injury, nerve palsies and compartment syndrome in the well leg [2][4]. People with spinal instability, fractures or osteoporosis are usually screened by clinicians before traction.

lead: A mechanical traction table is a motorised table that applies a controlled longitudinal pulling force to the spine, usually through harnesses at the pelvis and chest. Clinics market this as non-surgical spinal decompression, and the DRX9000 is one widely known device of the type.[1] People who care about standing height and posture discuss it as a way to decompress the discs and to present at the full length of the spine, which can make someone look taller and more upright.[3]

Two different devices share the name. The clinical decompression table is used in physiotherapy and chiropractic care for back and neck conditions, while the orthopaedic operating-room traction table holds a leg in position during hip and femur surgery and has no connection to height.[2][10] Height communities discuss the first kind, often alongside hanging, inversion and stretching.[9]

Research on clinical traction centres on pain and disc height. A 2010 cohort of 30 patients treated with a DRX9000 course reported both reduced pain and greater disc height on CT.[1] Wikipedia's summaries of reviews describe short-term pain relief from mechanical traction in some radiculopathy patients, with more mixed longer-term results.[4][5] Daily changes in body height, around 1.5 cm in one study of 100 children from morning to late afternoon, are the physiological backdrop for interest in decompression.[3]

chain: Spine sits at fuller length with better posture
angle.text: People use traction to decompress the spine so that discs sit at their fullest height and posture is more upright. Any change shows up as a small difference in measured or apparent standing height or carriage, not a change in bone length.

paras: A mechanical traction table has a split table, a pelvic harness and a thoracic harness, with a motor that varies the pulling force over a session. The pull can be continuous or intermittent. Spinal traction is described in physical therapy for cervical and lumbar disorders such as radiculopathy and stenosis.[4]

Non-surgical spinal decompression is a term used for traction-based care and is distinct from surgical decompression of the spine, which includes microdiscectomy and laminectomy.[5] Traction as a general concept has a long history; Wikipedia shows an early Greek traction device from a Byzantine edition of Galen's work, dated to the 2nd century AD, and describes skin traction, skeletal traction and spinal traction as the main types.[4]

Adult height is determined mainly by genetics, with twin studies estimating 60-80 percent heritability, and growth ends at roughly 18-19 for boys and 15-16 for girls.[3] What traction and decompression interact with is the soft part of stature: height varies over a day, and one study found 100 children averaged about 1.54 cm lower at 4-5 p.m. than in the morning; exercise before measurement lowers the reading and prolonged lying raises it.[3] Disc height also declines over a lifetime through dehydration and degeneration.[3]

Proponents therefore frame decompression as a way to hold the spine at its longest, rested length and to relax the back so standing posture is taller. Reported effects in the clinical literature are about disc height measured on CT in patients with herniation rather than standing stature in healthy adults.[1]

Wikipedia's article on spinal decompression reports that a 2022 meta-analysis found mechanical traction outperformed conventional physiotherapy in the short term but not in all studies longer than six months, and cites a 2021 meta-analysis supporting physiotherapy for prolapsed lumbar discs.[5] The traction article reports that supine lumbar traction has relieved short-term pain in radiculopathy, that a 2020 review found mechanical traction outperformed manual and continuous outperformed intermittent, and that its cited title describes the effect as statistically significant but not clinically relevant.[4] Three 2017 studies reportedly found increased nutrient and water flow into discs after traction; the article suggests inconsistent results may reflect variable force, rhythm, duration and frequency.[4]

Researchers have also studied who responds: a completed registered study examined whether a manual unloading test could predict responders to mechanical traction in low back pain.[13] A registered Polish study (NCT04507074) gave 30 minutes of continuous lumbar traction daily for four weeks to people with and without obesity who had chronic low back pain, measuring blood markers, spinal mobility and pain; no results have been posted to the registry.[7]

The same phrase refers to orthopaedic operating tables that hold a limb under traction for fracture fixation, hip arthroscopy and some hip replacements.[2][14] A systematic review and network meta-analysis of 43 randomised trials compared hip replacement through the direct anterior approach with and without a traction table, finding about 102 mL more blood loss with the table.[6] A meta-analysis of seven studies in femoral nailing found manual traction shortened operative time compared with the table without changing blood loss, fracture healing time or malunion rate.[11] These devices are not used for height.

Height-focused users describe decompression as a way to counter daily disc compression and to support posture, usually alongside hanging, inversion or stretching.[9] Inversion therapy, hanging by the ankles or feet on a table or boots, is described by Wikipedia as a form of spinal traction that proponents say briefly widens spaces between vertebrae and eases nerve root pressure; the article reports most people see no gain in recovery and that the main benefit is that it feels pleasant while happening.[9]

Proponents see a rested, decompressed spine as the basis for measuring and presenting at full height, and combine it with posture work and core strengthening. Because the largest daily height difference is reversible and returns with loading, community discussion usually focuses on short-term measured or apparent height rather than permanent growth.[3]

A retrospective cohort of 30 patients (mean age 65) who completed a six-week DRX9000 course reported pain falling from 6.2 to 1.6 on a 0-10 scale and CT disc height rising from 7.5 mm to 8.8 mm; the two changes were modestly correlated (r = 0.36), and the authors called for a randomized trial.[1]

Reviews summarised on Wikipedia report short-term pain relief from mechanical traction in radiculopathy and mixed longer-term results.[4][5] No published trial has measured a permanent change in adult standing height from traction tables.

Clinic traction is generally used for back and neck conditions, and clinicians screen for contraindications such as instability, fracture or osteoporosis. Inversion therapy is reported to be unsuitable for people with heart disease, high blood pressure, glaucoma or pregnancy, and users commonly report ankle discomfort within minutes; a 10-minute maximum is recommended.[9]

In surgery, traction tables have documented complications including injury to the perineal skin and soft tissue, neurological impairment and compartment syndrome of the well leg.[2] A review reported pudendal nerve palsy in 1.9 percent to 27.6 percent of patients after orthopaedic procedures using a traction table, mostly transient, with excessive or prolonged traction against the perineal post suggested as a mechanism.[8] An electrophysiology study examined pudendal neuropathy following traction.[12]

timeline.event: An early Greek traction device is depicted in a Byzantine edition of Galen's work.[4]
Electrophysiological analysis of pudendal neuropathy after surgical traction is published.[12]
BMC study of DRX9000 course links restored disc height with less discogenic low back pain; review of traction-table complications in orthopaedic surgery.[1][2]
Registered study begins on predicting responders to mechanical traction.[13]
Review reports pudendal nerve palsy rates of 1.9-27.6 percent after traction-table surgery.[8]
Registered trial of traction in people with obesity and chronic low back pain begins in Poland.[7]
Meta-analysis reports mechanical traction beating physiotherapy in the short term for pain.[5]
Network meta-analysis of 43 trials compares hip replacement with and without a traction table.[6]

lore.intro: Height forum users mention traction and decompression tables alongside hanging and inversion as ways to maximise measured height; the discussion is largely anecdotal and the claims are about short-term spinal length and posture.[9]

claims.claim: Decompression restores lost disc height and adds measurable stature
claims.believers: Proponents say that discs compressed by daily load can be re-expanded by traction, giving a taller morning-style height on demand.[3]
claims.experts: A cohort of back-pain patients reported greater CT disc height after a six-week DRX9000 course; no published study measures lasting adult height gain.[1]

claims.claim: Traction improves posture so a person looks taller
claims.believers: Users say a decompressed spine and relaxed back muscles let them stand more upright.
claims.experts: Reviews describe short-term pain relief from traction rather than posture or stature outcomes.[4][5]

claims.claim: Spinal traction lengthens the spine permanently
claims.believers: Some height-community posters describe traction as a route to extra height.
claims.experts: Adult height is mainly genetic and growth ends in the late teens; daily height variation is reversible and about 1.5 cm in a study of children.[3]

claims.claim: Inversion or hanging gives the same decompression as a table
claims.believers: Users treat hanging and inversion as a free equivalent of clinic traction.[9]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes inversion as a form of spinal traction whose main reported benefit is that it feels pleasant, with cardiac and eye contraindications.[9]

claims.claim: Traction relieves back pain and so supports better carriage
claims.believers: Clinic users and physiotherapists report short-term pain relief.[4]
claims.experts: A 2020 review's cited title calls the pain effect statistically significant but not clinically relevant; a 2022 meta-analysis found short-term benefit over physiotherapy.[4][5]

claims.claim: Operating-room traction tables are a stronger version of clinic decompression
claims.believers: Some people note that surgical tables apply heavy limb traction and wonder whether that equals stronger decompression.
claims.experts: Orthopaedic reviews describe these tables as positioning devices for hip and femur procedures, with documented perineal injury, nerve palsy and compartment syndrome.[2][8]
